explanations.explanation: Zechariah, Elizabeth's husband and a priest (Luke 1:5). Verse 40 says Mary entered his home and greeted Elizabeth. She walks in and says hello. Me? I'd still be circling the block, squinting at my phone and saying 'It said turn left at the oak tree.'

I get why Joseph came to mind, friend. He's the man Mary is engaged to (Luke 1:27). But the text says she entered the home of Zechariah. Zechariah is Elizabeth's husband, a priest (Luke 1:5), and Joseph isn't in this scene at all.

Simeon is a name for later, baker. He's a man in Jerusalem who shows up further along in Luke (Luke 2:25). In this visit, Mary walks into the home of Zechariah, Elizabeth's husband and a priest (Luke 1:5). Simeon isn't named in this scene.

explanations.answer: Her baby leaps in her womb
explanations.explanation: Verse 41 says it plain: when Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, the baby leaped in her womb. The greeting reached her and the baby leaped, just like that. I've seen dough rise slow, but this is a whole different speed.
It's the opposite, baker. Luke 1:41 says, 'the baby leaped in her womb.' Nothing in the text says the baby went still. The moment Mary's greeting arrives, there's movement.

Nothing in the text says Elizabeth's strength left her. What it says is that the baby leaped, and Elizabeth was filled with the Holy Spirit (Luke 1:41). That's the whole moment, and it's all happening at once.

True. Elizabeth says, 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!' (Luke 1:42). Same breath, same exclamation, both blessings back to back. The fruit of Mary's womb is her baby. She doesn't make Mary wait for the second blessing.

Actually, it's true, friend. Elizabeth says, 'Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb!' (Luke 1:42). The fruit of Mary's womb is her baby. So Elizabeth blesses Mary and the baby in one loud sentence.

Elizabeth says it herself: 'And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?' She doesn't say 'little Mary' or 'that nice visitor.' She says the mother of my Lord. That's a big title for someone standing at her door. When I get a visitor at the bakery I just say 'Come in, mind the flour,' so Elizabeth is clearly the better host.

explanations.answer: A prophet of the Most High
explanations.explanation: That's a good title, baker, but Elizabeth doesn't use it for Mary. She says, 'the mother of my Lord' (Luke 1:43). That's the title she gives Mary in this moment. Keep your ears on those exact words.

That title never comes up in this passage, friend. What Elizabeth says is 'the mother of my Lord' (Luke 1:43). She says it right in the middle of her question about why she's so honored. It's a short phrase, but she says it loud.

Joy, baker. Elizabeth says, 'the baby in my womb leaped for joy' (Luke 1:44). She's the one telling us what that leap meant. And it's the same kind of leap I do when someone says the oven's ready, except my base makes it a very loud landing.
Fear is a natural guess when something suddenly moves, friend. But Elizabeth says, 'the baby in my womb leaped for joy' (Luke 1:44). She names the feeling herself, and it's not fear. It's joy.
Elizabeth doesn't call it pain, baker. She says, 'the baby in my womb leaped for joy' (Luke 1:44). She tells us what the leap was, and she says joy. No pain anywhere in her words.

explanations.answer: Believing the Lord's word to her will be fulfilled
explanations.explanation: Elizabeth says, 'Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord's word to her will be fulfilled.' That's the reason she gives for the blessing. It's about believing what the Lord said to Mary. Believing is a lot harder than baking a batch, and I still burn the first tray.

explanations.answer: Traveling all the way to the hill country
explanations.explanation: Mary does hurry to the hill country (Luke 1:39), so I see the pull of that answer. But when Elizabeth gives the reason for the blessing, she doesn't mention the trip. She says, 'Blessed is she who has believed…' (Luke 1:45).

explanations.answer: Coming from the royal house of David
explanations.explanation: Elizabeth doesn't mention David or any royal family in her words, friend. She says, 'Blessed is she who has believed that the Lord's word to her will be fulfilled.' That's the blessing she gives, and it rests on believing. Everything else in that sentence is the Lord's word coming true.

explanations.answer: The humble state of His servant
explanations.explanation: Mary says, 'He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant.' She calls herself His servant, and she says God looked with favor on her humble state. That's the reason she gives for her rejoicing. I've spent years pressed flat in the back of a drawer, so humble state is a phrase I understand.

explanations.answer: The long prayers of His servant
explanations.explanation: Mary never mentions prayers here, baker. She says, 'He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant' (Luke 1:48). What God looked on is her humble state.

explanations.answer: The good works of His servant
explanations.explanation: Mary doesn't list any good works, friend. She says God 'has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant' (Luke 1:48). Her reason for rejoicing starts with what God did, not with a résumé.
Not quite, baker. Mary says, 'From now on all generations will call me blessed.' That's way bigger than one town. All generations is a LOT of people to have talking about you.

False, and Mary says so herself: 'From now on all generations will call me blessed.' No town limit anywhere in that sentence. Generation after generation, that's the reach she describes. So it's far wider than one town.
You got it, baker. Mary says, 'the Mighty One has done great things for me.' She names who did it, and it isn't herself. Then she adds, 'Holy is His name.' (Luke 1:49)

An angel did bring Mary the news. The angel Gabriel spoke to her (Luke 1:26-33). But when Mary talks about who did the great things, she says, 'the Mighty One has done great things for me' (Luke 1:49).
No king gets any credit in Mary's song, friend. She says, 'the Mighty One has done great things for me' (Luke 1:49). The great things come from Him alone.
You got it, baker. Mary says, 'His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation' (Luke 1:50). It goes down the line, one generation after another. She puts no number on it.
One lifetime would be a short stretch, baker. Mary says, 'His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation' (Luke 1:50). It keeps going from one generation to the next.

Forty years shows up in other Bible stories, friend, like Israel's forty years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2), but it's not in Mary's words. She says God's mercy extends 'from generation to generation' (Luke 1:50). There's no number on it.
Exalted is right, baker. Mary says God 'has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble' (Luke 1:52). Rulers come down, and the humble go up. That's the flip she describes.
Ignored is the opposite of what Mary says, baker. She says God 'has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble' (Luke 1:52). The humble get lifted up, not left alone.
Mary doesn't say tested, friend. The line is that God 'has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble' (Luke 1:52). Exalted means lifted up high.

True. Mary says, 'He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty.' Both halves are in the same verse. She puts the two side by side. The hungry get filled, and the rich leave empty.

It's true, baker. Mary says God 'has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty' (Luke 1:53). The second half is right there in the verse. Hungry ones get filled, and the rich go away empty.

You got it, baker. Mary says God helped Israel 'as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.' The mercy matches what He promised. She says He did it remembering to be merciful (Luke 1:54-55).
Warned doesn't fit here, baker. Mary says God helped Israel 'as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever' (Luke 1:55). The word is promised, and it comes with mercy.

Commanded is a real Bible word, friend, but it's not the one Mary uses. She says God remembered to be merciful 'as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever' (Luke 1:55). What He gave them was a promise.
